items.title: Lawrence Duhé Interview, 1957-06-09
items.q: Always played the lead, and Sidney was the hot man.

ctx.x: Some really, about 23, I think. Yeah. Oh, I was going to ask, I always wondered, you know, I mentioned to Mr. Bro the other day, too, when I was talking to him about when you had two clarinets in the band, you and Sidney, you played the lead, or did one play the lead?

Always played the lead, and Sidney was the hot man. He was the hot man. Always the hot man. Always was Peter. And you played more of the straight melody. Straight to let them know what's coming on, because he never could read, see, at that time. Yeah. But the minute you played it once over, that's all he tells you, let me have it. A whole lot of it he takes, too, I'm talking about. Oh, he's a great clarinetist. Oh, yeah.
Well, he's the best in the business for second, man. I'm telling you.

items.title: Lawrence Duhé Interview, 1960
items.q: I admire Sidney Bershaw. In fact, he was with me and we fell out on that account because I read and he didn't read but he could outplay me.

ctx.x: Mr. Dewey, would you tell us some of the fine players that played with you or that you knew while you were in Chicago?

Well, I left New Orleans with Sugar Johnny, and he got in bad health, and I switched to Mud Carry. After Mud Carry, the climate was too cold. He dropped me in Chicago, came back to New Orleans and sent King Oliver with me. So King Oliver stuck with me a while later, then he sent Armstrong later. Mr. Dewey, what did you think about Armstrong? I mean, as much as you know about him, what do you think about him? Greatest. One in the world greatest. Do you like his style of playing? Oh, yes. I really do. Did he play…
Mr. Dewey, a while ago, we did not ask you any questions at all about your family background, but would you tell me, were your parents and were all the people in your family Catholic?
